item.title: How to Turn Small Talk Into Deep Conversation
item.description:
Social Life

How to Turn Small Talk Into Deep Conversation

Is small talk a barrier to deep conversation, or could it be the gateway?

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Ordinary conversations often reveal subtle clues about what someone finds meaningful or important.
  • Research suggests that follow-up questions increase likability by communicating interest and responsiveness.
  • The goal in conversation is to notice openings for depth, not force every chat to be deeper.

Think of those conversations that never seem to get beyond the surface.

How's work? Good.

How was your weekend? Nice.

Been up to much lately? The usual.

Now think of the conversations that make you lose track of time.

The ones where one story leads to another, where you find yourself genuinely fascinated by what someone has to say, where you walk away feeling like you understand a little more about who they are.

What Makes These Conversations So Different?

We often assume it's the subject matter—that to have more meaningful conversations, we need to skip the small talk and start asking deeper questions.

But what if small talk isn't the obstacle to deep conversation, but the very thing that makes it possible?

Imagine Walking Into a Dark Room

You have no idea what's inside. There might be paintings on the walls, bookshelves full of fascinating stories, or doors leading into entirely different rooms.

But you can’t see anything clearly. You don’t know what’s there.

So you use your flashlight to scan the room, allowing yourself to discover what's there.

And when something catches your attention, you move closer, examine it from different angles, and begin to discover details you couldn't see from a distance.

That’s Precisely What Small Talk Is For

By asking a variety of surface-level questions, you’re using your flashlight to scan the room.

When you come across a topic that seems to spark the conversation, you know you’ve found something worth picking up and learning more about.

You ask deeper questions, seeking to explore this topic from different sides.

Go deep enough, and you may even learn why it matters to the person you’re speaking with and what that says about them.

The Art of Knowing What to Dive Deep Into

Consider how two conversations can begin in exactly the same way, yet end up somewhere entirely different:

Source: Dr Manu Sidhu / Made with ChatGPT

You can spend hours talking with someone, collecting one piece of information after the next, yet walk away feeling like you barely got to know them.

So how do you know what to dive deep into so the conversation moves somewhere more interesting?

You don’t need to introduce some profound philosophical question. You simply need to notice an interesting detail, and probe further:

Source: Dr Manu Sidhu / Made with ChatGPT

Rather than constantly moving from one topic to another, recognise an opportunity to move further into something that seems to:

  • Make them come alive—a change in tone, facial expression, enthusiasm
  • Matter to them—something they emphasise, linger on, or reveal a feeling about
  • Make you want to learn more—something that sparks your own curiosity

The skill isn't necessarily asking better opening questions. It's asking better follow-up questions.

Often, that might simply mean repeating back the interesting signal you noticed (in the example above: “Your first proper holiday in ages?”).

What Makes for a Good Follow-up Question?

A good follow-up question follows what the other person has given you reason to explore.

Consider the difference between these questions:

  • What do you do for work? → What drew you towards that kind of work?
  • Where did you grow up? → What was it like growing up there?
  • What do you enjoy doing? → What is it about that activity that you find so rewarding?
  • What are you planning next? → What makes that something you want to pursue?

The first question gathers information about someone's life.

The second begins to explore their experiences, motivations, feelings, and values.

This makes the shift from learning about someone to understanding them.

The Perfect Question

There are countless lists online promising the perfect set of questions to spark meaningful conversation, some of which may be useful.

But perhaps we're placing too much emphasis on what to ask next, and too little on what someone has just told us.

That’s where you’ll find your cue for something worth diving deep into.

In fact, in a series of studies, psychologists found that people who asked more follow-up questions tended to be better liked by their conversation partners. Why? Because those questions communicated that they were listening, interested, and responsive.1

Not Every Conversation Needs to Be Deep

Sometimes the setting isn't appropriate.

Sometimes a lighthearted chat is all that’s needed.

And sometimes an attempted follow-up receives a short answer that tells us the other person would rather move on.

That’s perfectly fine.

The aim isn't to make every conversation deep, but to recognise when depth is possible and take that opportunity when the moment feels right.

The Next Time You Find Yourself Making Small Talk

Imagine you're holding that flashlight. Start by shining it around, asking surface-level questions.

Notice what makes them come alive, what seems to matter to them, and what interests you.

When you discover something worth exploring, stop moving from topic to topic.

Dive deeper. Ask questions that cover every angle. Seek to understand why it matters.

That's when small talk stops being a barrier to deep conversation and becomes the gateway to it.

item.title: Peer Victimization Impacts Teens’ Self-Portrayals Later
item.description:
Adolescence

Peer Victimization Impacts Teens’ Self-Portrayals Later

Students’ self-portrayals worsen when victimized by their peers over time.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Our study followed a group of more than 300 Brazilian adolescents over the course of two school years.
  • Earlier reports of being victimized by peers was tied to worse self-portrayals the following year.
  • The effect of previous peer victimization was explained by stability in victimization over time.
  • This study highlights the long-term consequences of being picked on by classmates.

One of the main developmental tasks of adolescence is to develop a strong and positive sense of self. However, many youth struggle to do so. These struggles are evidenced in students’ negative self-portrayals. Negative self-portrayals reflect the unfavorable beliefs adolescents hold about themselves, including feelings of shame, self-doubt, or inadequacy, or perceptions that they are not good enough. In our recently published paper, we examined how peer victimization one year earlier combined with concurrent peer victimization predicted Brazilian youths' negative self-portrayal even after controlling for earlier values.

How peer victimization affects adolescent views of themselves

Our research team followed more than 300 adolescents from Curitiba, Brazil, over two school years to better understand how their experiences with peers relate to changes in the way they view themselves. The main variable of interest for our study was students’ negative self-portrayal. In other words, we wanted to better understand why some young people have poor views of themselves. This involved asking them about how they saw themselves, using, for instance, statements such as “I think I'm not a good person.” We then came back a year later asking the students to tell us again how they felt about themselves. In general, the majority of participants (64.8 percent) tended to disagree with these statements, suggesting that most youth feel positively about themselves. Not surprisingly, earlier scores of negative self-portrayals were strongly related to later scores, highlighting how stable this construct is over time.

The other variable we were interested in assessing was peer victimization. Here too, we asked participants to self-report, specifically how often they were teased, insulted, and made fun of by their peers, among other items. Whereas a sizable proportion of students (60.30 percent) reported “never” or “almost never,” this also meant more than a third (39.70 percent) reported “almost always” or “always.” Those adolescents who reported being victimized by their peers were significantly more likely to view themselves negatively, with 16 to 25 percent sharing overlap between the two constructs.

Scatterplot of the relationship between Year 1 peer victimization (earlier) and Year 2 negative self-portrayal (later). More victimization was related to worse self-portrayals (black line). Also included are histograms of the proportion of scores for both variables.
Source: Jonathan Santo

Our results revealed a number of notable effects. First off, reports of peer victimization during the first school year were linked to more negative self-portrayals over a year later (depicted above). This effect persisted even when we controlled for those who had worse self-portrayals a year earlier. However, the relationship between earlier victimization and later worse self-portrayals disappeared when including later peer victimization (i.e., happening concurrently). In other words, the stability of peer victimization and its cumulative impact over time explained the link to poor self-portrayals.

The results from this study underscore that peer victimization is not an isolated factor related to how adolescents see themselves and habitual victimization can compound those effects. All told, the models we tested using these data were able to explain 40.10 percent of the differences in students’ views of themselves.

Remaining questions

Despite these findings, some questions remain that the current study couldn’t answer. Perhaps most importantly, previous studies have shown that the relationship between victimization and self-portrayals is bi-directional. To explain, even though we looked at how victimization predicts later self-portrayals, other research has shown youth with poor views of themselves are also more likely to be targeted for victimization by their peers. Our study couldn’t disentangle causes from effects.

While these findings replicate those of other studies, using a Brazilian sample also allows us to ask how these results would apply to adolescents from other parts of the world. Much of previous psychological research has come from samples in North America and Europe, making it difficult to relate to students’ experiences in other parts of the world. We’d love to conduct this same study in other countries to better understand the similarities and differences across samples.

Where do we go from here?

Our goal with this research was to better understand the challenges that adolescents face in their interactions with their peers at school. Although our study did not test any interventions or treatments, parents and educators can take several practical steps:

  • Pay attention to how adolescents talk about themselves. Statements such as "I’m not good enough” or “nobody likes me” might reveal struggles with self-worth. Rather than dismissing these feelings, listen with empathy and find out what might be contributing to these negative self-portrayals.
  • Encourage adolescents to explore their interests, develop new skills, and celebrate their personal accomplishments.
  • Support adolescents in developing healthy relationships and friendships with trusted adults. Feeling accepted, understood, and valued can provide an important source of reassurance, especially for young people experiencing peer victimization.

Ultimately, stopping peer victimization and bullying is only part of the picture. As parents, teachers, practitioners, and educators, we must empower adolescents to recognize that their self-worth is not determined by how others treat them.

Source: Sheri McVay, used with permission

About the co-author: Sheri McVay is a developmental psychologist with a master’s degree from the University of Nebraska at Omaha (UNO). She is currently pursuing a doctoral degree at UNO, with her research focused on peer relations, traditional bullying, and cyber victimization among children and adolescents.

item.title: Understanding Others Is the Key to Better Communication
item.description:
Persuasion

Understanding Others Is the Key to Better Communication

Effective communication relies on your knowing that it's not about you.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Communication is a critical skill that seems rarely to be explicitly taught.
  • Communication is an essential part of any business activity.
  • Certain tools and approaches can increase influence.

I had been a practicing psychologist for more than a decade when I had a critical realization. No one in my academic journey through leading psychology schools had ever addressed communication. And my experience was now revealing that communication should be one of the main topics in medical, or any, education, especially when the job entails critical personal interaction.

I decided to research the topic and eventually wrote the book Power Talk: The Art of Effective Communication. The effort changed how I approached my clients. Now, not only was I trying to understand their perceptions and feelings from a diagnostic viewpoint but also from a motivational one. I needed to understand where they were at and adjust my messaging accordingly.

It still stuns me to this day how little education there is on communication generally, given that it is an absolutely critical life skill, not just a business one.

The Universal Importance of Communication

Almost every endeavor that involves working with others relies on effective communication. One of the biggest reasons patients change doctors is that they don’t feel the doctor understands or relates to them. We’ve all encountered the doctor who is just telling you what to do and treating you like just another number.

Conversely, some of us have encountered doctors who have a great “bedside manner”; in other words, they really try to understand you and address you accordingly. I believe that this difference in approach does impact outcome.

The same could be applied to teachers, managers, nurses—you name it. Genuinely investigating where people are at not only helps in the planning of messaging but also in connection. And connection clearly matters.

Specific Communication Tools

One of the greatest advocates of understanding others' viewpoints and where they were coming from was the psychiatrist Milton Erickson, who brilliantly used this approach to change rigidly held beliefs. Jay Haley's book Uncommon Therapy explains and shares Erickson’s exceptional work.

Erickson couched his work in terms of hypnotherapy, but his fundamental tools do not require hypnosis as such. A person doesn’t have to be in a hypnotic state to defend and uphold their most important perceptions and ideas. This point was highlighted by Robert Cialdini, a psychologist and communication expert whose book Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion identifies several key principles, like social proof, that can be used to change someone’s perceptions. Now, unfortunately, some of these principles, like social proof, have been hijacked by scamming advertisers who show fake photos as signs of their product’s worth. However, it’s not the principle’s fault that they are misappropriated in this way.

Aren’t Sales People the Best Communicators?

Even in fields like sales, where you might assume communication is a required trait, good communication isn't necessarily a given. In his recent book Uncertainty: Why Deals Stall: The Human Side of Buying and the 13 Buyer Uncertainties That Cost You Wins, marketing guru Bill Zujewski shows that even in the sales industry, many people don't understand where the potential buyer is coming from or the real factors behind their decision-making. These are often not about the product per se, but the potential social, reputational, political, and emotional impact of the purchase.

This understanding about communication is even more relevant today, when primitive, binary thinking only leads to disconnection and anger (see politics and social media).

Preparing for an Important Conversation

There are some simple questions that can help you prepare for any conversation in which you desire a specific outcome, i.e., getting the other person to agree with you in some way.

  • What is the purpose of this communication?
  • What do I want the outcome to be?
  • How might the other person respond?
  • What is important to the other person in this context?
  • What core principles do they hold?
  • How can I frame the conversation to embrace their core beliefs?

We tend to be egotistical in our communication and make the mistake of not trying to understand the other person or figure out how to really engage them.

As I wrote in Power Talk: “People aren’t logical; they’re psychological, often with the emphasis on the psycho.”
